svg.aria-label: Diagram: Google Cloud labels as per-resource metadata versus tags as first-class resources with their own IAM roles, inheritance down the hierarchy, and a separate list of policy engines that can enforce on them
svg.title: Labels versus tags in Google Cloud: metadata written on a resource against a resource the platform reads from
svg.text: A label is written on a resource. A tag is a resource.
Metadata that describes, against metadata that decides. Everything else follows from that one difference.
Label — metadata on one resource
A key-value pair you assign to a resource. Typed on
the resource, with no prerequisite of any kind.
No inheritance. It exists where it was set.
Cannot be used to set conditions on policies.
Up to 64 per resource. Keys 1 to 63 characters and
never empty; values may be empty, up to 63.
Lowercase letters, numerics, underscores, dashes.
No IAM of its own — editing a label is editing
the resource that carries it.
Billing: labels, project.labels, system_labels.
Tag — three discrete resources
Tag keys, tag values and tag bindings are all
resources, defined under an organization or project.
Key and value must exist before anything can
carry them. There is no ad-hoc tag.
Descendants inherit an attached value by default.
Max 50 key-value pairs per resource. Max 1000 keys
per org or project; 1000 predefined values per key.
Its own roles: Tag Viewer, Tag User to attach,
Tag Administrator to define.
Billing: tags — key, value, namespace, inherited.
Inheritance: one binding, a whole branch
Organization → folder → project → resource.
Bind environment=production once on the folder and
everything below it carries the value, including
resources created long afterwards.
A descendant may override with the same key.
Retirement runs in one direction only
1. Remove every binding from every resource.
2. Delete the values under the key.
3. Only then can the key itself be deleted.
A label is removed by editing the resource, and
nothing else is affected.
Attaching a tag and enforcing on it are two different support lists
Many services accept tags on their resources. Only three engines read one to make a decision: Identity and Access
Management, the Organization Policy Service, and Virtual Private Cloud for network firewall policies.
Resources not listed as supported by policy engine services cannot be targeted directly for conditional enforcement.
So a tag can sit on a resource, appear in billing, look correct, and still be unable to deny anything on it.
The two-question test, applied once per piece of metadata
Will a policy read it? If yes it is a tag, and it must be defined before anything can carry it.
Must it apply to a whole branch at once? If yes it is a tag, because inheritance is the only mechanism that does that.
Everything else — owner, ticket reference, application name, anything high-cardinality — is a label.
